title: E-E-A-T in Practice: How to Show Experience on Every Page
excerpt: E-E-A-T is not a score you can raise with a badge. Here is what it really means and the on-page signals that show experience and earn trust on every page.
meta_title: E-E-A-T Checklist: How to Show Experience and Trust
meta_description: What E-E-A-T really is, why it is not a single ranking factor, and a practical checklist of author bios, evidence, sources and dates that show trust.
key_takeaways: E-E-A-T comes from Google's Search Quality Rater Guidelines and is not a single ranking factor, but Google's systems look for signals that align with it.
Trust is the most important part of E-E-A-T, and experience, expertise and authority all contribute to it.
Real bylines that link to author pages are one of the simplest ways to show who is behind your content.
Original photos, screenshots and test results show first-hand experience that summaries and AI drafts cannot copy.
Only change an updated date when the content has substantially changed, and keep visible dates consistent with your structured data.
content_html:
Say you run a small home renovation business and publish a guide to sealing a leaky shower. The advice is solid. But the page has no author name, no photos of an actual shower, no date, and the "About" link goes to a single paragraph of marketing copy. From the outside, it looks exactly like a page written by someone who has never held a caulking gun, and that is an E-E-A-T problem.

That gap between what you know and what the page shows is what E-E-A-T is about. Google uses the term to describe the kind of content its systems try to reward: content that demonstrates experience, expertise, authoritativeness and trust.

There is a lot of confusion around it, too. Some people treat E-E-A-T as a score you can raise with a few badges. Others dismiss it because it is "not a ranking factor".

This guide sits between those two views. You will learn what E-E-A-T actually is, where it comes from, and a practical set of on-page signals you can add to any page, from author bios and first-hand evidence to honest dates and sources.

What E-E-A-T actually is (and what it is not)

E-E-A-T stands for Experience, Expertise, Authoritativeness and Trustworthiness. The framework comes from Google's Search Quality Rater Guidelines, a long document that human raters use to evaluate the quality of search results.

The first "E" is the newest. Google added Experience to the framework in December 2022, to recognize content created by someone who has actually used the product, visited the place or done the thing.

The key point: E-E-A-T is not a single ranking factor you can measure, but Google's ranking systems look for signals that line up with it. Google's own page on creating helpful, reliable, people-first content says this directly. It also says that search raters have no control over how pages rank, and that of the four parts, trust is the most important.

So think of E-E-A-T as a description of a good page, not a checklist that triggers a boost. If you are new to how Google evaluates sites in general, start with our beginner's guide to how SEO works and come back here.

In practice, the four parts break down like this:

  • Experience: the author has first-hand involvement with the topic (used it, tested it, lived it).
  • Expertise: the author has the knowledge or skill the topic needs.
  • Authoritativeness: the author or site is a known, go-to source for the topic.
  • Trust: the page is accurate, honest, safe and transparent about who is behind it.

Why E-E-A-T matters more for some topics

Not every page needs the same level of proof. A recipe for banana bread and an article about medication dosages are held to very different standards.

Google calls the high-stakes category "Your Money or Your Life" (YMYL): topics that could significantly affect people's health, financial stability, safety, or the welfare of society. For these, Google says its systems give even more weight to content with strong E-E-A-T, and that the content should be highly accurate and consistent with established expert consensus.

Here is how that plays out for a hypothetical small business site:

  • A bakery's post about its favorite sourdough starter: experience matters most. Photos and honest notes from the bakers do the job.
  • An accountant's post on small business tax deadlines: this is YMYL. It needs a named, qualified author, current dates, and links to the official tax authority.
  • A pet store's guide to toxic foods for dogs: also YMYL (animal health). Cite veterinary sources and say who reviewed the advice.

Action: list your ten most important pages and mark which ones touch health, money, safety or legal matters. Those get the full treatment below first.

Signal 1: Real bylines and author pages

Google's helpful content guidance asks a simple question: is it self-evident to visitors who created the content? It goes on to ask whether pages carry a byline where one might be expected, and whether bylines lead to more information about the author.

A byline is cheap to add, and it answers the first question every skeptical reader has: who wrote this?

A useful author page includes:

  • The person's real name and a real photo.
  • Their role and what they actually do day to day ("Licensed electrician, 12 years in residential wiring" beats "Passionate content creator").
  • Relevant qualifications, certifications or memberships, only if they exist.
  • Links to their professional profiles or other work.
  • A list of the articles they have written on the site.

Say your plumbing company blog is written by the owner and reviewed by a senior technician. Show both: "Written by Sam Lee, owner. Reviewed by Priya Shah, master plumber." Each name links to a short author page.

Do not invent people. Google explicitly warns against deceptive authorship, such as fabricated creator profiles with made-up names or AI-generated headshots. A company byline ("The Acme Plumbing team") is far better than a fake expert.

If you use Article structured data, you can also mark up the author name and author URL so the byline is machine-readable. Our guide to adding schema markup with JSON-LD shows how a block like that is put together.

Signal 2: First-hand evidence on the page

Experience is the easiest part of E-E-A-T to show and the hardest for a competitor to copy. If you have done the thing, prove it on the page.

Evidence that works:

  • Original photos: your team on the job, the product on your workbench, the before and after.
  • Screenshots: the actual settings screen, the actual report, with your own data.
  • Test results: what you measured, how, and what happened. Include the boring details (dates, conditions, versions).
  • Specifics only a practitioner knows: the step that usually goes wrong, the tool you stopped using and why.

Compare two sentences from a hypothetical lawn mower review. "This mower is powerful and easy to use" could have been written by anyone. "On our half-acre test lawn, the battery lasted 41 minutes with the grass at about 10 cm, and the bag filled twice" could only come from someone who mowed the lawn.

This matters even more if you draft with AI tools. An AI draft has no experience to share, so it is up to you to add it. Our walkthrough on turning a raw AI draft into human content covers how to edit for exactly this.

Signal 3: Sources you would stake your name on

Trust is built on accuracy, and accuracy is easier to judge when readers can check your claims.

Link every statistic, threshold or rule to the place it came from, and prefer the primary source. If you mention a legal deadline, link the government page, not a blog that summarized it. If you quote a study, link the study.

  • Remove any statistic you cannot trace to a source. Unverifiable numbers hurt trust more than they help.
  • Name the source in the sentence ("according to the national weather service...") so readers do not have to click to know who said it.
  • Re-check sources when you update a page. Links die and guidance changes.

Signal 4: About, contact and policy pages

Trust is also a site-level question. A reader who likes your article will often click "About" before buying from you or acting on your advice.

A trustworthy small business site usually has:

  • An About page that names the people behind the business, how long it has operated and where it is based.
  • A Contact page with real ways to reach you: a physical address if you have one, a phone number, an email address.
  • Policies that fit the site: returns and shipping for a shop, an editorial or review policy for a content site, a privacy policy for anyone collecting data.
  • Clear disclosure of affiliate links or sponsored content.

The rater guidelines put particular weight on who is responsible for a website and how customers can get help, especially for sites that take payments. An online store with no contact details is a red flag for real shoppers too.

Signal 5: Honest dates and real updates

Showing when a page was published or last updated helps readers judge whether advice is current. It also helps Google, which looks at several factors to estimate a page's date.

Google's guidance on showing byline dates in search recommends a clear, visible date on the page, matched by datePublished and dateModified in your structured data.

Only change the "updated" date when you have substantially changed the content. Google's helpful content page specifically lists changing dates to make pages seem fresh, when the content has not substantially changed, as a warning sign.

A good update note looks like this: "Updated 3 March: added the new filing deadline and removed the section on the retired form." It tells the reader what changed and why it matters to them.

An E-E-A-T checklist for any page

Use this as a pass over each important page. It works alongside a broader pre-publish on-page SEO checklist, which covers titles, headings and internal links.

CheckWhat good looks like
WhoVisible byline linking to a real author page; reviewer named for YMYL topics
ExperienceAt least one piece of original evidence: photo, screenshot, measurement or worked example
SourcesEvery number and rule linked to a primary source
Site trustAbout and contact pages one click away; relevant policies in place
DatesVisible published or updated date that matches structured data and reflects real changes
PurposeThe page exists to help a reader, not just to rank for a keyword

The last row comes from Google's "Who, How, and Why" questions. "Who" is the author, "How" is how the content was made (including any use of automation), and "Why" is whether the main reason the page exists is to help people.

E-E-A-T and AI search

The same signals carry over to AI features in search. Google's guidance for those features emphasizes unique, first-hand content over summaries of what is already online, which is the "Experience" part of E-E-A-T in different words.

If you want to go further, our guide on appearing in Google AI Overviews explains what Google has said about AI search and what you can safely ignore.

The bottom line

E-E-A-T is not a switch you flip or a score you can check. It is Google's description of content that deserves trust, and the practical work is making the experience and care behind your pages visible: real authors, original evidence, cited sources, clear contact details and honest dates.

Start with the pages where accuracy matters most to your readers, especially anything touching health, money or safety, and work outward from there. Every signal you add helps real visitors as much as it helps search engines.

Your next step: pick your single most important article today, add a real byline that links to an author page, and add one piece of first-hand evidence (a photo, screenshot or measurement) that only your business could have produced.

faqs.question: Is E-E-A-T a Google ranking factor?
faqs.answer: Not as a single measurable factor. Google says E-E-A-T itself is not a specific ranking factor, but its systems use a mix of signals that help identify content with good experience, expertise, authoritativeness and trust. Improving those signals tends to make pages more useful to readers as well.

faqs.question: What does the extra E in E-E-A-T stand for?
faqs.answer: The first E stands for Experience. Google added it to its quality rater guidelines in December 2022 to recognize content created by people with first-hand experience of the topic, such as someone who has actually used a product or visited a place.

faqs.question: Do I need an author bio on every blog post?
faqs.answer: Google encourages accurate bylines wherever readers would expect them, and most blog posts fall into that category. A short byline linking to a fuller author page is usually enough. If several people work on a post, you can name both the writer and the reviewer.

faqs.question: Can AI-written content have good E-E-A-T?
faqs.answer: AI tools have no first-hand experience, so an unedited AI draft rarely shows it. If you use AI to help write, add your own evidence, check every fact against a source, and make sure a real, accountable person stands behind the page.

faqs.question: What are YMYL pages?
faqs.answer: YMYL stands for Your Money or Your Life. It covers topics that could significantly affect a person's health, finances, safety or the welfare of society. Google holds these pages to a higher standard of accuracy and trust.
